# Tempered Perfect Lattices in the Binary Case

**Authors:** Erik Bahnson Mark McConnell Kyrie McIntosh ††thanks: Department of Mathematics, Princeton University. E-mails: ebahnson@alumni.princeton.edu, markwm@princeton.edu, kyriem@alumni.princeton.edu. MSC2020: 11F75 (primary), 11E16, 11F25, 11H55, 11R29 (secondary).

## Abstract

A new algorithm for computing Hecke operators for $\mathrm{SL}_{n}$ was introduced in [14]. The algorithm uses tempered perfect lattices, which are certain pairs of lattices together with a quadratic form. These generalize the perfect lattices of Voronoi [17]. The present paper is the first step in characterizing tempered perfect lattices. We obtain a complete classification in the plane, where the Hecke operators are for $\mathrm{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{Z})$ and its arithmetic subgroups. The results depend on the class field theory of orders in imaginary quadratic number fields.

## 1 Introduction

Lagrange and Gauss knew that a plane lattice $L$ with a quadratic form could have interesting number-theoretic structure. This paper describes the number-theoretic structure of pairs of lattices $M\subset L$ . Our methods are elementary, but class field theory is needed to tell the whole story.

The motivation is to study a new algorithm [14] for computing Hecke operators. Let $\mathbb{G}$ be the algebraic group $\mathrm{SL}_{n}$ of a finite-dimensional division algebra (possibly commutative) over $\mathbb{Q}$ . Let $G$ be the real points of $\mathbb{G}$ , and let $X$ be the symmetric space for $G$ . Let $\Gamma\subset G$ be an arithmetic subgroup. We study the cohomology $H^{i}(\Gamma\backslash X;\rho)$ with coefficients in suitable finite-dimensional coefficient systems $\rho$ . A family of Hecke operators acts on this cohomology. Many authors have given algorithms for computing these Hecke operators in different settings and for different ranges of the degree $i$ . (A short list relevant to this paper is [13, 16, 3, 10].) The new algorithm in [14] works in complete generality in the setting we have described— $\mathrm{SL}_{n}$ of any division algebra, with arbitrary coefficients $\rho$ , and in all degrees $i$ . See [9, §2] for an exposition of [14] in the most common case $G=\mathrm{SL}_{n}(\mathbb{R})$ .

The new algorithm uses tempered perfect lattices. These are certain pairs of lattices $M\subset L$ together with a quadratic form. They generalize the perfect forms introduced by Voronoi [17]. Section 2 will define these terms.

The definition of a tempered perfect lattice uses only Euclidean geometry. When we run the algorithm of [14], however, the data shows that tempered perfect lattices also depend on number theory. This paper is the first step in understanding and characterizing tempered perfect lattices. For this first step, we restrict to $G=\mathrm{SL}_{n}(\mathbb{R})$ . In fact, we restrict to $\mathrm{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{R})$ , because the classical theory of binary quadratic forms is so rich.

For $\mathrm{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{Z})$ , there is essentially one Hecke operator $T_{\ell}$ at each prime $\ell$ , and these $T_{\ell}$ generate the algebra of all Hecke operators. In any approach to Hecke operators for $\mathrm{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{Z})$ , $T_{\ell}$ is defined using lattices $L$ and sublattices $M\subset L$ of index $\ell$ . We assume $M\subset L$ has prime index $\ell$ throughout the paper.

We now briefly describe the different families of tempered perfect lattices for $n=2$ . We refer to figures that come later in the paper. In the figures, points of $L$ are dots $\cdot$ , points of $M$ are circled dots $\odot$ , and the quadratic form is the standard dot product. The temperament $\tau$ is defined to be the ratio of the lengths of the shortest non-zero vectors in $M$ and $L$ , respectively. This is the ratio of the radii of the two circles in each figure. When there are $s$ pairs $\pm v$ of vectors of $L-M$ on the inner circle, and $s^{\prime}$ pairs of vectors of $M$ on the outer circle, we call the form an $s$ -and- $s^{\prime}$ form.

The only perfect plane lattice, up to rotation and scaling, is the hexagonal lattice. One family of tempered perfect lattices is the $3$ -and- $3$ forms, where $L$ and $M$ are both hexagonal lattices, a snowflake within a snowflake. Figure 2 shows the 3-and-3 form with index $\ell=7$ . We identify $L$ with the Eisenstein integers, the ring $\mathbb{Z}[\omega]$ where $\omega=e^{2\pi i/3}$ . Figure 2 arises because the prime 7 splits as $(2-\omega)(2-\bar{\omega})$ . Here $2-\omega$ is one of the three pairs of shortest vectors in $M$ , and all these vectors have length $\tau=\sqrt{7}$ .

Figure 3 is a $3$ -and- $1$ form. Here $L$ is again $\mathbb{Z}[\omega]$ . The shortest non-zero vector $v\in M$ still has length $\sqrt{7}$ , but in any lattice basis $\{v,w\}$ of $M$ , $w$ is strictly longer than $\sqrt{7}$ . Thus $M$ has less symmetry than $L$ . The 3-and-1 forms are determined partly by number theory and partly by geometry. Theorem 1 and Algorithm 1 give their precise characterization.

A lattice is well rounded [1] if the non-zero lattice vectors of minimal length contain a basis. In any well-rounded plane lattice (besides the hexagonal lattice), the shortest non-zero vectors comprise two pairs $\pm v,\pm w$ , and $\{v,w\}$ is a lattice basis. When $L$ and $M$ are both well rounded with two pairs of minimal vectors each, then $M\subset L$ is a $2$ -and- $2$ form.

A familiar well-rounded lattice is the square lattice $L$ , which may be identified with the Gaussian integers $\mathbb{Z}[i]$ . In Figure 4, $M$ is $1+4i$ times $L$ . Then $M$ is also a square lattice, sitting in $L$ at an angle. This is a 2-and-2 form. The index is the norm $|1+4i|^{2}=17$ . The temperament is $\tau=\sqrt{17}$ .

The 2-and-2 forms become more interesting when $M$ has a different shape from $L$ . Figure 5 shows the first example, which occurs for $\ell=23$ . The angle between the vectors in a well-rounded basis of $L$ (the points on the inner circle) is not equal to the angle for $M$ (the outer circle). For the first time, $\tau^{2}$ is not an integer: it is $\frac{17\cdot 23}{19}$ . We soon discover that class field theory determines 2-and-2 forms. $L$ and $M$ are fractional ideals in the quadratic number field $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-1155})$ , where $1155=3\cdot 5\cdot 7\cdot 11$ . The class group of $K$ has order eight, and the seven primes $3,5,7,11,17,19,23$ encountered in this example lie in exactly the seven non-trivial classes of the class group (Table 1). Well-rounded fractional ideals of $K$ lie in the classes for $17$ and $19$ and in no others. The class of $23$ times the class of $19$ is the class of $17$ , and this is why $\tau^{2}=\frac{17\cdot 23}{19}$ has a 2-and-2 form.

We now summarize our main theorems characterizing 2-and-2 forms, theorems that are stated and proved in Sections 8 and 9. We show that $L$ and $M$ are proper ideals in an order $\mathcal{O}$ of discriminant $D<0$ in a quadratic number field. $\mathcal{O}$ depends on $\ell$ , $L$ , and $M$ , but it is the same for $M$ as for $L$ . Hence the 2-and-2 forms are controlled by arithmetic in the class group of $\mathcal{O}$ . Theorem 2 shows that only finitely many orders $\mathcal{O}$ will yield 2-and-2 forms for a given index $\ell$ , and it gives a bound on the discriminant $D$ in terms of $\ell$ . Theorem 3 is a converse: if an order $\mathcal{O}$ has a 2-and-2 form for a certain $\ell$ , the same $\mathcal{O}$ will yield 2-and-2 forms for infinitely many $\ell^{\prime}$ , those coming from the Chebotaryov Density Theorem applied to the class of $\ell$ in $\mathcal{O}$ . In Section 9.2, we show why the discriminants $D$ for 2-and-2 forms will always be a product of comparatively small prime factors.

There are many directions for future work growing out of this paper. One is to classify tempered perfect lattices for $\Gamma\subseteq\mathrm{SL}_{2}(\mathcal{O}_{F})$ , where $\mathcal{O}_{F}$ is the ring of integers of a number field $F$ . This would connect with the literature on Hecke operators for Bianchi modular forms and Hilbert modular forms. (As a short list, see [2, 11] and the references therein.) A second direction is to classify tempered perfect forms for $\Gamma\subseteq\mathrm{SL}_{n}(\mathbb{Z})$ for $n>2$ , especially for $n=3$ and $4$ . This would involve pairs of projective configurations, as in [12].

## 2 Background

### 2.1 Lattices and pairs of lattices

We view $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ as a space of row vectors. When $\{v,w\}$ is a basis of $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ , a lattice $L$ is the set of $\mathbb{Z}$ -linear combinations of $v$ and $w$ . We call $\{v,w\}$ a $\mathbb{Z}$ -basis of $L$ .

Let $L_{0}$ be the standard copy of $\mathbb{Z}^{2}$ with basis $\{(1,0),(0,1)\}$ . Let $G=\mathrm{GL}_{2}(\mathbb{R})$ (not $\mathrm{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{R})$ as in the Introduction). The subgroup of $G$ that stabilizes $L_{0}$ is $\Gamma_{0}=\mathrm{GL}_{2}(\mathbb{Z})$ . Every lattice $L$ has the form $L_{0}\,g$ for $g\in G$ . When we have a specific $g$ in mind, we say the rows of $g$ are a distinguished basis of $L$ .

A homothety is multiplication of $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ by a positive real scalar. The homotheties form a group $\mathbb{R}_{+}$ .

By $(L,M)$ we denote a pair $M\subset L$ where $L$ is a lattice and $M$ is a sublattice of finite index. $M$ has the form $Lg$ for some integer matrix $g$ with $[L:M]=|\det g|$ . In the special case $M_{0}=L_{0}\,g$ for an integer matrix $g$ , the group $\Gamma=\Gamma_{0}\cap g^{-1}\Gamma_{0}\,g$ is the common stabilizer in $G$ of $L_{0}$ and $M_{0}$ , the stabilizer of the pair $(L_{0},M_{0})$ . This $\Gamma$ has finite index in $\Gamma_{0}$ .

### 2.2 Pairs of lattices of prime index

Throughout the paper, let $\ell$ be a prime number. A lattice $L$ contains exactly $\ell+1$ sublattices $M$ of index $\ell$ , namely

$$ \begin{bmatrix}\ell&0\\
0&1\end{bmatrix}L,\qquad\begin{bmatrix}1&k\\
0&\ell\end{bmatrix}L $$

where $k=0,\dots,\ell-1$ . It is easy to show that $\Gamma_{0}$ acts transitively on the sublattices of $L_{0}$ of index $\ell$ .

Suppose $M_{0}$ has basis $\{(1,0),(0,\ell)\}$ . The stabilizer of $(L_{0},M_{0})$ is the classical congruence subgroup

$$ \Gamma_{0}(\ell)=\left\{\left.\begin{bmatrix}a&b\\
c&d\end{bmatrix}\in\Gamma_{0}\,\right|\,b\equiv 0\bmod\ell\right\} $$

whose index in $\Gamma_{0}$ is $\ell+1$ .

An element $v\in L$ is primitive if $v$ generates $(\mathbb{R}v)\cap L$ .

#### Lemma 1.

A given primitive vector in a lattice $L$ is contained in one and only one sublattice $M$ of index $\ell$ .

#### Proof.

It suffices to consider a primitive $(x,y)\in L_{0}$ . Take integers $s,t$ with $sx+ty=1$ . Multiplying by $\begin{bmatrix}x&y\\ -t&s\end{bmatrix}^{-1}\in\Gamma_{0}$ , we may assume the primitive vector is $(1,0)$ . In (1), only $\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\ 0&\ell\end{bmatrix}$ has $(1,0)$ in the $\mathbb{Z}$ -span of its rows. ∎

### 2.3 Quadratic forms

Throughout the paper, let $\langle(x_{1},y_{1}),(x_{2},y_{2})\rangle=\begin{bmatrix}x_{1}&y_{1}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\ 0&1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x_{2}\\ y_{2}\end{bmatrix}$ be the standard dot product on $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ . The subgroup of $G$ preserving $\langle\,,\,\rangle$ is the group $\mathrm{O}_{2}(\mathbb{R})$ of orthogonal matrices. Let $X=G/\mathrm{O}_{2}(\mathbb{R})\mathbb{R}_{+}$ ; this is the symmetric space from the Introduction.

Each lattice $L=L_{0}\,g$ carries the inner product $\langle\,,\,\rangle$ . We can view this from a second perspective: not a fixed inner product on a space of lattices, but a fixed lattice carrying a space of inner products. If we change coordinates by $g^{-1}$ , then $L$ becomes the fixed lattice $L_{0}$ , and the matrix of the inner product becomes $A=g\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\ 0&1\end{bmatrix}g^{T}=gg^{T}$ , where T is the transpose. This defines a quadratic form $\begin{bmatrix}x&y\end{bmatrix}A\begin{bmatrix}x\\ y\end{bmatrix}$ on $L_{0}$ . In this paper, quadratic forms will always be positive definite.

We consider two quadratic forms to be equivalent if they differ by a homothety. Our $X$ is the space of quadratic forms modulo homotheties. Going back to the lattice perspective, $X$ is the space of lattices with a distinguished basis, in which two lattices are considered equivalent if one can be carried to the other by an orthogonal transformation and a homothety.

### 2.4 Reduced bases

The minimal vectors of $L$ are the $v\in L-\{0\}$ where $\|v\|^{2}=\langle v,v\rangle$ attains its minimal value. Minimal vectors occur in pairs $\pm v$ .

The lattice $L$ has a Minkowski reduced basis, or just reduced basis, constructed as follows [4, (2.7.7)]. Let $v\in L$ be a minimal vector. Let $w\in L$ have minimal length among vectors for which $\{v,w\}$ is linearly independent over $\mathbb{R}$ . Then $\{v,w\}$ is a $\mathbb{Z}$ -basis of $L$ , and the angle $\theta$ between $v$ and $w$ satisfies $\pi/3\leqslant\theta\leqslant 2\pi/3$ . (We emphasize that this is for $n=2$ . For $n\geqslant 5$ , naively picking the shortest lattice vectors in successive dimensions $1,2,\dots,n$ may not produce a lattice basis [7, (15.10.1)].)

In Figure 1, we reproduce the standard picture. Rescale $L$ by a homothety so that the minimal vector $v$ has length 1, and rotate to carry $v$ to $(1,0)$ . Then the lattice basis $\{v,w\}$ is reduced if and only if $\pm w$ is in the shaded region. This region is a fundamental domain for $\mathrm{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{Z})\backslash X$ .

*Figure 1: A reduced basis $\{v,w\}$ has $v=(1,0)$ and $w$ in the shaded region.*

When $n=2$ , a lattice is well rounded if, among its minimal vectors, there are two vectors forming a $\mathbb{Z}$ -basis of the lattice. This $\mathbb{Z}$ -basis is Minkowski reduced, and its $w$ is on the bottom circular edge of the shaded region in Figure 1. When the angle is exactly $\pi/3$ or $2\pi/3$ , we get the hexagonal lattice. No lattice for $n=2$ has four or more pairs of minimal vectors.

### 2.5 Tempered perfect forms

We refer to [14] for rather lengthy technical material on temperaments, the well-tempered complex and its cell decomposition, and critical temperaments, as well for how the complex is used to compute Hecke operators. This relies on [1] for sets of weights, the well-rounded retract, and perfect forms. Assuming this technical background, a tempered perfect lattice is by definition a $0$ -dimensional cell in the well-tempered complex. A tempered perfect form is a quadratic form on $L_{0}$ corresponding to a tempered perfect lattice.

We now give an equivalent, self-contained definition of a tempered perfect form.

#### Definition 1.

Let $\ell$ be a prime number. Let $L_{0}=\mathbb{Z}^{2}$ and let $M_{0}$ be a sublattice of $L_{0}$ of index $\ell$ . A positive definite quadratic form $A$ on $L_{0}$ is a tempered perfect form if there exist non-empty subsets $S\subset L_{0}-M_{0}$ and $S^{\prime}\subset M_{0}-\{0\}$ such that

(i) $vAv^{T}=1$ for all $v\in S$ ;

(ii) $vAv^{T}>1$ for all $v\in L_{0}-M_{0}$ with $v\notin S$ ;

(iii) $vAv^{T}$ have a common value $u$ for all $v\in S^{\prime}$ , with $u\geqslant 1$ ;

(iv) $vAv^{T}>u$ for all $v\in M_{0}-\{0\}$ with $v\notin S^{\prime}$ ;

(v) if $B$ is any quadratic form satisfying (i)–(iv) with common value $u^{\prime}$ , then $B=A$ and $u=u^{\prime}$ .

The temperament of a tempered perfect form is $\tau=\sqrt{u}$ .

We use the constant $1$ in (i)–(ii) to normalize the form in its homothety class. If $\tau=1$ , we recover Voronoi’s definition of perfect form [17, §§1–5], in which $S\cup S^{\prime}$ is the (single) set of minimal vectors.

Similarly, $L$ is a tempered perfect lattice if there is a sublattice $M\subset L$ of index $\ell$ , and non-empty sets $S\in L-M$ , $S^{\prime}\subset M-\{0\}$ , such that (i)–(v) hold taking $A$ to be the standard dot product. We will go freely back and forth between the perspectives of tempered perfect lattices and forms for the rest of the paper.

#### Definition 2.

An $s$ -and- $s^{\prime}$ form is a tempered perfect form where $s$ (resp., $s^{\prime}$ ) is the number of pairs $\pm v$ in $S$ (resp., $S^{\prime}$ ).

Since well-rounded lattices have either two or three pairs of minimal vectors,

#### Definition 3.

A doubly well-rounded form is an $s$ -and- $s^{\prime}$ form with $s\geqslant 2$ and $s^{\prime}\geqslant 2$ .

## 3 Structure of tempered perfect forms

### 3.1 Rationality of tempered perfect forms

Write a tempered perfect form as $ax^{2}+bxy+cy^{2}$ for $(x,y)\in L_{0}$ . The matrix of the form is $\begin{bmatrix}a&b/2\\ b/2&c\end{bmatrix}$ . All we know at first is that $a,b,c\in\mathbb{R}$ . The next proposition generalizes Voronoi’s result that perfect forms are rational [17, §5].

#### Proposition 1.

For a tempered perfect form $ax^{2}+bxy+cy^{2}$ , the quantities $a$ , $b$ , $c$ , and $\tau^{2}$ are in $\mathbb{Q}$ .

#### Proof.

We use the notation of Definitions 1 and 2. Let $(x_{i},y_{i})\in\mathbb{Z}^{2}$ be the vectors in $S$ followed by $S^{\prime}$ , with only one from each pair $\pm v$ . Parts (i) and (iii) of the definition state

$$ \begin{bmatrix}x_{1}^{2}&x_{1}y_{1}&y_{1}^{2}&0\\
\vdots&\vdots&\vdots\\
x_{s}^{2}&x_{s}y_{s}&y_{s}^{2}&0\\
x_{s+1}^{2}&x_{s+1}y_{s+1}&y_{s+1}^{2}&-1\\
\vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\vdots\\
x_{s+s^{\prime}}^{2}&x_{s+s^{\prime}}y_{s+s^{\prime}}&y_{s+s^{\prime}}^{2}&-1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}a\\
b\\
c\\
u\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1\\
\vdots\\
1\\
0\\
\vdots\\
0\end{bmatrix}. $$

Part (v) states there is a unique solution for $a$ , $b$ , $c$ , $u$ when we regard the $x_{i}$ and $y_{i}$ as given. Parts (ii) and (iv) do not affect the uniqueness statement, since they are strict inequalities (open conditions). Thus the system of linear equations (2) must have a unique solution. The coefficient matrix on the left has entries in $\mathbb{Z}$ , as does the vector on the right. Hence the solution has entries in $\mathbb{Q}$ . By definition, $\tau^{2}=u$ . ∎

Since the matrix in (2) has rank $4$ ,

#### Corollary 1.

In an $s$ -and- $s^{\prime}$ form, $s+s^{\prime}\geqslant 4$ .

### 3.2 The boundary temperaments

The temperament $\tau=1$ is special. The only perfect lattice for $n=2$ is the hexagonal lattice, so perfect forms for $\tau=1$ have three pairs of minimal vectors. Either one or none of these pairs will be in $M$ . By Corollary 1, no form for $\tau=1$ is tempered perfect.

The temperament $\tau=1$ is a boundary case because $\tau\geqslant 1$ by (iii). The next lemma shows that $\tau=\ell$ is the other boundary case.

#### Lemma 2.

In any tempered perfect form, $\tau\leqslant\ell$ .

#### Proof.

Suppose $\tau>\ell$ . Let $v$ be the shortest non-zero vector in $L$ . Then $vAv^{T}=1$ by (i), so $(\ell v)A(\ell v)^{T}=\ell^{2}<u$ . But $\ell v\in M$ , so $(\ell v)A(\ell v)^{T}=\ell^{2}\geqslant u$ by (iii)–(iv), a contradiction. ∎

Consider an $s$ -and- $s^{\prime}$ form in the boundary case $\tau=\ell$ . If $v\in S$ , then $\ell v\in S^{\prime}$ since $u=\ell^{2}$ . Hence $s\leqslant s^{\prime}$ . We cannot have $s\geqslant 2$ , for then $s^{\prime}\geqslant 2$ , and $M$ would contain a well-rounded sublattice of index $\ell^{2}$ ; the index $[L:M]$ is prime, hence $M$ would contain some other vector shorter than squared-length $\ell^{2}$ , contradicting the definition of $u$ .

We can have tempered perfect forms with $\tau=\ell$ with $s=1$ . Corollary 1 implies these are 1-and-3 forms, where $M$ is the hexagonal lattice.

Turning away from the boundary cases, we now suppose $1<\tau<\ell$ . All the minimal vectors for $L$ are in $S$ but not in $S^{\prime}$ . The shortest non-zero vector in $M$ is always in $S^{\prime}$ . Thus an $s$ -and- $s^{\prime}$ form has $s\geqslant 1$ and $s^{\prime}\geqslant 1$ . For doubly well-rounded forms, $S$ contains a Minkowski reduced basis of $L$ , and $S^{\prime}$ contains a Minkowski reduced basis of $M$ .

### 3.3 Enough minimal vectors implies tempered perfect

We will need the following converse to Proposition 1.

#### Proposition 2.

If a rational quadratic form $A$ satisfies parts (i)-(iv) of Definition 1 with $s+s^{\prime}\geqslant 4$ , then it also satisfies part (v) and is thus a tempered perfect form.

#### Proof.

It suffices to prove that (2) has a unique solution for $a,b,c,u$ when $s+s^{\prime}\geqslant 4$ .

From Section 2.4, $s\leqslant 3$ and $s^{\prime}\leqslant 3$ . First suppose $s=3$ . Then $L$ is the hexagonal lattice. After a change of coordinates, $A=x^{2}-xy+y^{2}$ . This determines $a$ , $b$ , and $c$ , and $u$ is determined from (iii) by any one of the vectors in $S^{\prime}$ . When $s^{\prime}=3$ , the proof is similar, interchanging the roles of $S$ and $S^{\prime}$ .

The remaining case is $s,s^{\prime}\geqslant 2$ . From Section 3.2, $1<u<\ell^{2}$ . We may change coordinates so that $L=L_{0}$ and $S=\{\pm v_{1},\pm v_{2}\}$ for $v_{1}=(1,0)$ and $v_{2}=(0,1)$ . Let $v_{3}=(x_{3},y_{3})$ , $v_{4}=(x_{4},y_{4})\in S^{\prime}$ with $v_{4}\neq\pm v_{3}$ . Because $u<\ell^{2}$ , $\ell v_{1}$ and $\ell v_{2}$ are not in $M$ , so $x_{3}$ , $y_{3}$ , $x_{4}$ , $y_{4}$ are all non-zero. Let $A=\begin{bmatrix}a&b/2\\ b/2&c\end{bmatrix}$ . We use $v_{1}$ and $v_{2}$ to deduce $a=c=1$ . Then $v_{3}Av_{3}^{T}=v_{4}Av_{4}^{T}=u$ . Since $\{v_{1},v_{2}\}$ is Minkowski reduced, $|b|\leqslant 1$ . As in (v), suppose $B=\begin{bmatrix}a^{\prime}&b^{\prime}/2\\ b^{\prime}/2&c^{\prime}\end{bmatrix}$ is an arbitrary quadratic form satisfying (i)–(iv). Then $a^{\prime}=a=1$ , $c^{\prime}=c=1$ , $|b^{\prime}|\leqslant 1$ , and $v_{3}Bv_{3}^{T}=v_{4}Bv_{4}^{T}=u^{\prime}$ . We have

$$ \displaystyle u \displaystyle=x_{3}^{2}+y_{3}^{2}+x_{3}y_{3}b \displaystyle u \displaystyle=x_{4}^{2}+y_{4}^{2}+x_{4}y_{4}b \displaystyle u^{\prime} \displaystyle=x_{3}^{2}+y_{3}^{2}+x_{3}y_{3}b^{\prime} \displaystyle u^{\prime} \displaystyle=x_{4}^{2}+y_{4}^{2}+x_{4}y_{4}b^{\prime}. $$

Subtracting,

$$ u-u^{\prime}=x_{3}y_{3}(b-b^{\prime})=x_{4}y_{4}(b-b^{\prime}). $$

If $b=b^{\prime}$ , then $u=u^{\prime}$ and we are done. So suppose $b\neq b^{\prime}$ . Then $x_{3}y_{3}=x_{4}y_{4}$ . From the first two equations in (3), $x_{3}^{2}+y_{3}^{2}=x_{4}^{2}+y_{4}^{2}$ . Changing the sign of $b$ if necessary, $x_{3}>0$ and $y_{3}>0$ . Considering the way a circle at the origin meets the hyperbola $xy=C$ for $C>0$ , we see there are only two possibilities, $(x_{3},y_{3})=(x_{4},y_{4})$ and $(x_{3},y_{3})=(y_{4},x_{4})$ . We have excluded the first possibility, so $x_{3}=y_{4}>0$ and $x_{4}=y_{3}>0$ . Interchanging $v_{3}$ and $v_{4}$ if necessary, we may assume $x_{3}>y_{3}>0$ .

Since $\{v_{3},v_{4}\}$ is a Minkowski reduced basis of $M$ , we have $\det\begin{bmatrix}x_{3}&y_{3}\\ y_{3}&x_{3}\end{bmatrix}=(x_{3}+y_{3})(x_{3}-y_{3})=\ell$ . Since $\ell$ is prime, $x_{3}+y_{3}=\ell$ and $x_{3}-y_{3}=1$ . Thus $\ell$ must be odd, $x_{3}=(\ell+1)/2$ , and $y_{3}=(\ell-1)/2$ . But then $v_{3}-v_{4}=(1,-1)\in M$ . Hence

$$ \begin{bmatrix}1&-1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1&b/2\\
b/2&1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1\\
-1\end{bmatrix}>u. $$

We deduce $2-b>u=x_{3}^{2}+y_{3}^{2}+x_{3}y_{3}b$ , or $2>\ell^{2}/2+1/2+(\ell^{2}+3)b/4$ , or $b<\frac{6-2\ell^{2}}{3+\ell^{2}}=\frac{12}{3+\ell^{2}}-2$ . Because $|b|\leqslant 1$ , we have $\frac{12}{3+\ell^{2}}-2\geqslant-1$ , which forces $\ell=3$ , $b=-1$ , $v_{3}=(2,1)$ , and $v_{4}=(1,2)$ . Changing coordinates so that the quadratic form becomes the standard dot product, we have arrived at the 3-and-3 form where $L$ and $M$ are both hexagonal lattices and $[L:M]=3$ , which is tempered perfect. ∎

## 4 Background on binary quadratic forms

Proposition 1 shows that, up to homothety, a tempered perfect form is a binary quadratic form $ax^{2}+bxy+cy^{2}$ with $a,b,c\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $\gcd(a,b,c)=1$ . The form can also be written $(a,b,c)$ . A form with $\gcd(a,b,c)=1$ is primitive. The discriminant of $ax^{2}+bxy+cy^{2}$ is $D=b^{2}-4ac$ . As we have said, all forms in this paper are positive definite; this implies $a>0$ , $c>0$ , and $D<0$ .

### 4.1 Binary quadratic forms and lattices

As in Section 2.3, $g\mapsto gg^{T}$ maps a lattice with distinguished basis to a quadratic form. The matrix of $ax^{2}+bxy+cy^{2}$ is $\begin{bmatrix}a&b/2\\ b/2&c\end{bmatrix}$ . Dividing by $a$ and solving $\begin{bmatrix}1&b/2a\\ b/2a&c/a\end{bmatrix}=gg^{T}$ for $g$ , we find one solution

$$ g=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\
b/2a&\sqrt{-D}/2a\end{bmatrix}. $$

(The general solution is $gk$ for $k$ orthogonal.)

A special property of $n=2$ is that these lattice bases can be understood using complex numbers. Identify $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ with $\mathbb{C}$ by $(x,y)\leftrightarrow x+yi$ . The bottom row of (4) is $\gamma=\frac{b+\sqrt{D}}{2a}$ , an element of the imaginary quadratic field $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{D})$ . The lattice $L=L_{0}\,g$ has distinguished basis $\{1,\gamma\}$ .

Quadratic forms $A$ , $A^{\prime}$ are equivalent if $MAM^{T}=A^{\prime}$ for some $M\in\mathrm{GL}_{2}(\mathbb{Z})$ . They are properly equivalent if we may take $M\in\mathrm{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{Z})$ .

### 4.2 Proper ideals and orders

A fractional ideal in $K$ is a finitely generated $\mathbb{Z}$ -submodule of $K$ that spans $K$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ . Fractional ideals are lattices. Fractional ideals $L_{1},L_{2}$ in $K$ are similar, denoted $L_{1}\sim L_{2}$ , if $L_{2}=\alpha L_{1}$ for some $\alpha\in K$ , $\alpha\neq 0$ . Similar fractional ideals correspond to the same quadratic form in $X$ .

An order $\mathcal{O}$ in a number field is a subring which contains $1$ and which spans the number field over $\mathbb{Q}$ . It is a lattice. $K$ has a unique maximal order $\mathcal{O}_{K}$ , its ring of integers.

The coefficient ring of a fractional ideal $L$ of $K$ is $\mathcal{O}_{L}=\{\alpha\in K\mid\alpha L\subseteq L\}$ . It is an order of $K$ . Similar fractional ideals have the same coefficient ring. $L$ is similar to an ideal $L^{\prime}\subseteq\mathcal{O}_{L}$ .

In quadratic fields, the orders have a particularly simple classification [4, §2.7]. Let $D$ be an integer which is not a square, and let $d$ be the squarefree part of $D$ . Let $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{D})=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{d})$ . Let $\beta=\sqrt{d}$ if $d\equiv 2,3\bmod 4$ and $\beta=\frac{1+\sqrt{d}}{2}$ if $d\equiv 1\bmod 4$ . Then $\mathcal{O}_{K}=\mathbb{Z}[\beta]$ . The discriminant of $\mathcal{O}_{K}$ is called the discriminant of $K$ , or the fundamental discriminant $d_{0}$ for $d$ . We have $d_{0}=4d$ if $d\equiv 2,3\bmod 4$ and $d_{0}=d$ if $d\equiv 1\bmod 4$ . The orders of $K$ are the rings $\mathcal{O}_{f}=\mathbb{Z}[f\beta]$ for positive integers $f$ ; here $f$ is called the conductor. The discriminant of $\mathcal{O}_{f}$ is $f^{2}d_{0}$ . Conversely, to each integer $D$ , there is at most one order of discriminant $D$ .

As in (4), the primitive form $ax^{2}+bxy+cy^{2}$ corresponds to the lattice $L$ with basis $\{1,\gamma\}$ with $\gamma=\frac{b+\sqrt{D}}{2a}$ . Here $\mathcal{O}_{L}$ has discriminant $D$ [4, p. 136].

An ideal $L\subseteq\mathcal{O}$ may have a coefficient ring strictly larger than $\mathcal{O}$ . We say $L$ is a proper ideal of $\mathcal{O}$ if it is an ideal of $\mathcal{O}$ and its coefficient ring equals $\mathcal{O}$ [8, p. 121]. A fractional ideal similar to a proper ideal is also called proper.

Let $L$ be a proper fractional ideal of $\mathcal{O}$ . Consider a matrix $B$ whose rows are a basis of $L$ expressed in coordinates with respect to a basis of $\mathcal{O}$ . Then $|\det B|$ does not depend on the choice of bases and is called the norm $N(L)$ of $L$ . If $L\subseteq\mathcal{O}$ , then $N(L)=[\mathcal{O}:L]$ . The norm is multiplicative: $N(L_{1}L_{2})=N(L_{1})N(L_{2})$ .

The product of proper fractional ideals $L_{1}$ , $L_{2}$ of $\mathcal{O}$ is a proper fractional ideal for the same $\mathcal{O}$ [4, §2.7.4]. If $\bar{L}$ is the image of $L$ under complex conjugation, then $L\bar{L}=N(L)\mathcal{O}$ , which means $\bar{L}$ is a multiplicative inverse for $L$ up to similarity. This shows the similarity classes of proper fractional ideals for $\mathcal{O}$ form an abelian group under multiplication, the (proper) ideal class group of $\mathcal{O}$ . This group is finite [4, p. 139].

Complex conjugation defines an involution $\mathcal{C}\mapsto\bar{\mathcal{C}}$ on ideal classes. An ideal class $\mathcal{C}$ is ambiguous11 1 “Gauss, writing in Latin, used the word anceps, meaning either ‘two-headed’ or ‘ambiguous’, and with deliberate reference to the Roman god Janus.” [5, p. 7] if $\mathcal{C}=\bar{\mathcal{C}}$ , or, equivalently, $\mathcal{C}^{2}=(1)$ .

### 4.3 Well-rounded ideal classes

If the fractional ideal $L$ is a well-rounded lattice, then any similar fractional ideal is well rounded. Well-roundedness depends only on the ideal class.

#### Proposition 3.

Let $\mathcal{O}$ be an order in an imaginary quadratic number field $K$ . Let $L$ be a proper fractional ideal of $\mathcal{O}$ that is well rounded. Then $L^{2}$ is principal.

#### Proof.

Let $\{v_{1},v_{2}\}$ be a well-rounded $\mathbb{Z}$ -basis of $L$ . Let $w=v_{1}+v_{2}$ . Let $V$ be the fractional ideal $V=w^{-1}L$ . Clearly $V^{2}$ is principal if and only if $L^{2}$ is. By definition, $v_{1}$ and $v_{2}$ have the same length in $\mathbb{C}$ . The generators $v_{1}/w$ and $v_{2}/w$ of $V$ have equal length, and they make equal and opposite angles with the real axis. Therefore $V=\bar{V}$ . Thus $V^{2}\sim V\bar{V}=(N(V))$ is principal. ∎

#### Corollary 2.

Well-rounded classes are ambiguous.

As for the converse, ambiguous classes are not well rounded in general. See Section 8.3.1.

### 4.4 Reduced forms

A primitive form $ax^{2}+bxy+cy^{2}$ is reduced [4, p. 149] if22 2 Other authors choose $b\geqslant 0$ in the boundary cases $|b|=a$ or $a=c$ .

$$ |b|\leqslant a,\mathrm{\ and\ }b\leqslant 0\mathrm{\ if\ either\ }|b|=a\mathrm{\ or\ }a=c. $$

The minimal non-zero value of this reduced form is $a$ . A well-known reduction algorithm converts any primitive form into a unique properly equivalent reduced form of the same discriminant. A form is reduced if and only if its distinguished lattice basis (4) is reduced. A major result is that (4) gives a bijection between the reduced forms of discriminant $D$ and the proper ideal class group for the order of discriminant $D$ [4, §2.7] [8, §2.A].

By [8, Lemma 3.10], a reduced form $(a,b,c)$ is ambiguous if and only if

$$ b=0,\mathrm{\ }b=-a,\mathrm{\ or\ }a=c. $$

For reduced lattice bases $\{1,w\}$ corresponding to these three cases, $w$ lies in Figure 1 as follows:

- • on the $y$ -axis in the center of the fundamental domain,

- • on a vertical edge of the fundamental domain, or

- • on the curved bottom edge of the fundamental domain.

We call a primitive form $(a,b,c)$ well rounded if the corresponding fractional ideal is well rounded. As we have said, well-roundedness depends only on the class.

#### Lemma 3.

A reduced form $(a,b,c)$ is well rounded if and only if $a=c$ .

#### Proof.

This follows from [4, §2.7.7] (the third bullet point above). ∎

Since a homothety does not change well-roundedness, the statement of Lemma 3 holds even if $(a,b,c)$ is not primitive.

## 5 Duality

Let $L$ be a lattice with inner product $\langle\,,\,\rangle$ . The dual of $L$ is $L^{*}=\{w\in\mathbb{R}^{2}\mid\langle v,w\rangle\in\mathbb{Z}$ for all $v\in L\}$ . If $L$ has $\mathbb{Z}$ -basis $\{v_{1},v_{2}\}$ , then $L^{*}$ is a lattice with $\mathbb{Z}$ -basis the dual basis $\{v_{1}^{*},v_{2}^{*}\}$ characterized by $\langle v_{i},v_{j}^{*}\rangle=\delta_{ij}$ (Kronecker delta). The double dual $L^{{*}{*}}$ is $L$ , canonically.

#### Lemma 4.

A plane lattice and its dual have $\mathbb{Z}$ -bases which differ from each other by a rotation and a homothety.

#### Proof.

Let $\{v_{1},v_{2}\}$ be any basis of the lattice. Say $\|v_{1}\|\leqslant\|v_{2}\|$ . Up to rotation and homothety, $v_{1}=(1,0)$ and $v_{2}=(x,y)$ with $y>0$ and $x^{2}+y^{2}\geqslant 1$ . The dual basis is $\{(1,-x/y)$ , $(0,1/y)\}$ . Calculation shows the second dual basis vector is shorter than the first. To preserve orientation, interchange the dual vectors and multiply the longer one by $-1$ , obtaining the basis $w_{1}=(0,1/y)$ , $w_{2}=(-1,x/y)$ of $L^{*}$ . Identify $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ with $\mathbb{C}$ as before. The ratio $v_{2}/v_{1}$ is $x+yi$ , and the ratio $w_{2}/w_{1}=(-1+(x/y)i)/(i/y)=x+yi$ . Since the ratios are equal, $\{v_{1},v_{2}\}$ and $\{w_{1},w_{2}\}$ differ only by a rotation and homothety. ∎

#### Corollary 3.

The dual basis of a reduced lattice basis is a reduced basis.

#### Corollary 4.

$L$ and $L^{*}$ have the same number of pairs of minimal vectors.

If $L=L_{0}\,g$ , then $L^{*}=L_{0}\,g^{*}$ for $g^{*}=(g^{-1})^{T}$ .

If $M\subseteq L$ are lattices, then $L^{*}\subseteq M^{*}$ and $[M^{*}:L^{*}]=[L:M]$ .

#### Proposition 4.

If $(L,M)$ is an $s$ -and- $s^{\prime}$ tempered perfect lattice of index $\ell$ and temperament $\tau$ , then $(M^{*},L^{*})$ is an $s^{\prime}$ -and- $s$ tempered perfect lattice of index $\ell$ and temperament $\ell/\tau$ .

#### Proof.

By Corollary 4, $M^{*}$ has $s^{\prime}$ pairs of minimal vectors and $L^{*}$ has $s$ pairs of minimal vectors. A quadratic form is rational if and only if its dual is rational. Proposition 2 then implies $(M^{*},L^{*})$ is a tempered perfect form of index $\ell$ .

We now consider the temperaments. When $\tau=1$ (resp., $\ell$ ), the lattice $L$ (resp., $L^{*}$ ) is hexagonal, and the result follows directly. Now assume $1<\tau<\ell$ . Let $\{v_{1},v_{2}\}$ be a reduced basis of $L$ and $\{w_{1},w_{2}\}$ a reduced basis of $M$ . The vectors $v_{1},v_{2},w_{1},w_{2}$ are all distinct. Suppose $\|v_{1}\|\leqslant\|v_{2}\|$ and $\|w_{1}\|\leqslant\|w_{2}\|$ . Let $v_{2}^{\perp}$ be the orthogonal projection of $v_{2}$ onto the line perpendicular to $v_{1}$ . Clearly $\|v_{1}\|\|v_{2}^{\perp}\|=\det L$ . Define $w_{2}^{\perp}$ similarly, with $\|w_{1}\|\|w_{2}^{\perp}\|=\det M$ . The proof of Lemma 4 shows that $\|v_{1}^{*}\|=1/\|v_{2}^{\perp}\|$ and $\|w_{1}^{*}\|=1/\|w_{2}^{\perp}\|$ . By definition, the temperament $\tau$ for $(L,M)$ is $\tau=\|w_{1}\|/\|v_{1}\|$ , and the temperament $\tau^{*}$ for $(M^{*},L^{*})$ is $\tau^{*}=\|v_{1}^{*}\|/\|w_{1}^{*}\|$ . We observe

$$ \tau^{*}=\frac{\|v_{1}^{*}\|}{\|w_{1}^{*}\|}=\frac{\|w_{2}^{\perp}\|}{\|v_{2}^{\perp}\|}=\frac{\det M/\|w_{1}\|}{\det L/\|v_{1}\|}=\frac{[L:M]}{\tau}. $$

∎

Consider a binary quadratic form with matrix $A=gg^{T}$ . The dual form has matrix $A^{*}=g^{*}(g^{*})^{T}$ . A calculation shows the dual form for $ax^{2}+bxy+cy^{2}$ is $cx^{2}-bxy+ay^{2}$ up to homothety. These two forms have the same discriminant.

## 6 Doubly well-rounded forms

A tempered perfect lattice is a pair $(L,M)$ where $L$ and $M$ are fractional ideals in the same imaginary quadratic field, possibly with different coefficient rings. We now prove that, for doubly well-rounded forms, $L$ and $M$ have the same coefficient ring. “Doubly well-rounded” includes 3-and-3 forms as well as 2-and-2 forms.

### 6.1 Coefficient ring of the lattice and sublattice

Consider a primitive reduced form $(a,b,c)$ on $L_{0}$ . Suppose this defines a doubly well-rounded form $(L_{0},M_{0})$ for some sublattice $M_{0}$ of index $\ell$ . Lemma 3 applied to $L_{0}$ shows the form is in fact $(a,b,a)$ with $\gcd(a,b)=1$ . Let $D=b^{2}-4a^{2}$ be the discriminant. When we restrict the form to the index $\ell$ sublattice $M_{0}$ , write it in coordinates $x,y$ with respect to some $\mathbb{Z}$ -basis of $M_{0}$ , and reduce it, it will have different coefficients $(u,v,w)$ , not necessarily primitive. Since $M_{0}$ is well rounded, the form is $(u,v,u)$ . In this situation, $\tau^{2}=u/a$ .

#### Proposition 5.

Consider a doubly well-rounded reduced form, with notation as above. Then $\gcd(u,v)=\ell$ . Letting $u_{1}=u/\ell$ and $v_{1}=v/\ell$ , the form $(u_{1},v_{1},u_{1})$ is a primitive and reduced form on $M_{0}$ of discriminant $D$ . The lattice and sublattice have the same coefficient ring. The temperament $\tau$ of this doubly well-rounded form satisfies

$$ \tau^{2}=\ell\frac{u_{1}}{a}. $$

#### Proof.

Temporarily change $(a,b,a)$ to a properly equivalent form $(a_{1},b_{1},c_{1})$ with $\ell\nmid a_{1}$ ; this is possible by [8, (2.25)]. The matrix of the form on $M_{0}$ is $H\begin{bmatrix}a_{1}&b_{1}/2\\ b_{1}/2&c_{1}\end{bmatrix}H^{T}$ , where $H$ is one of the $\ell+1$ matrices in (1). [5, Prop. 7.3] addresses this situation. It shows that the form on $M_{0}$ has discriminant either $D$ or $\ell^{2}D$ . Furthermore, it shows that the discriminant is $D$ if and only if the form on $M_{0}$ is primitive, and that in the imprimitive case the form is $\ell$ times a primitive form of discriminant $D$ . Thus to prove our proposition, it suffices to show that the form on $M_{0}$ does not have coefficient ring of discriminant $\ell^{2}D$ .

Consider the chain of inclusions $\ell L_{0}\subset M_{0}\subset L_{0}$ . Both inclusions have index $\ell$ , so the result from [5] applies to each inclusion. The discriminant of the coefficient ring for $M_{0}$ is equal to either 1 or $\ell^{2}$ times the discriminant of the coefficient ring for $L_{0}$ , and the discriminant of the coefficient ring for $\ell L_{0}$ is equal to either 1 or $\ell^{2}$ times the discriminant of the coefficient ring for $M_{0}$ . But the coefficient rings for $L_{0}$ and $\ell L_{0}$ are equal, since the lattices are homothetic. Thus all three coefficient rings are the same. ∎

### 6.2 Characterization of doubly well-rounded forms by ideals

Since well-roundedness depends only on the ideal class, we would like to use ideal classes to compare the two lattices in a doubly well-rounded form.

#### Proposition 6.

Given a doubly well-rounded form, if $\mathcal{O}$ is the common coefficient ring of its lattices $(L,M)$ , then $\mathcal{O}$ contains a prime proper ideal $\mathfrak{p}_{\ell}$ of norm $\ell$ , and $M=\mathfrak{p}_{\ell}L$ .

#### Proof.

The multiplicative inverse of $L$ is proper and equals $\frac{1}{N(L)}\bar{L}$ . Thus $\mathfrak{p}_{\ell}=\frac{1}{N(L)}\bar{L}M$ is a proper fractional ideal of $\mathcal{O}$ satisfying $\mathfrak{p}_{\ell}L=M$ . Since $M\subset L$ , we have $\mathfrak{p}_{\ell}\subseteq\mathcal{O}$ , and we may drop the word “fractional” for $\mathfrak{p}_{\ell}$ . Since $[L:M]=\ell$ , we have $N(\mathfrak{p}_{\ell})=\ell$ . The ideal $\mathfrak{p}_{\ell}$ is prime, indeed maximal, because $|\mathcal{O}/\mathfrak{p}_{\ell}|$ is prime. ∎

Combining Propositions 5 and 6, we have characterized doubly well-rounded forms in terms of the class group, as follows.

#### Corollary 5.

Let $\mathfrak{a}$ be an ideal of $\mathcal{O}$ in a well-rounded class $\mathcal{C}$ . Suppose $\mathfrak{p}_{\ell}$ is a prime proper ideal of $\mathcal{O}$ of norm $\ell$ , and suppose $\mathfrak{p}_{\ell}\mathfrak{a}$ is in a well-rounded class $\mathcal{C}^{\prime}$ . Then $(L,M)=(\mathfrak{a},\mathfrak{p}_{\ell}\mathfrak{a})$ is doubly well rounded. Conversely, every doubly well-rounded form occurs in this way.

## 7 Tempered perfect forms from the Eisenstein integers

Because of duality, it suffices to consider $s$ -and- $s^{\prime}$ forms where $s\geqslant s^{\prime}$ . By Corollary 1, $s+s^{\prime}\geqslant 4$ . In this section we characterize the temperaments $\tau$ of 3-and- $s^{\prime}$ forms. The techniques differ from those for 2-and-2 forms, since for 3-and- $s^{\prime}$ forms we work exclusively in the hexagonal lattice, the Eisenstein integers $\mathbb{Z}[\omega]$ . We will return to 2-and-2 forms in Section 8.

We always identify vectors $v\in\mathbb{R}^{2}$ with the corresponding $z\in\mathbb{C}$ . The norm $N(z)$ of $z\in\mathbb{C}$ is its squared length $\|v\|^{2}=\langle v,v\rangle=|z|^{2}$ . When $z\in\mathbb{Z}[\omega]$ (or, in the later sections, in other orders $\mathcal{O}$ ), we also identify $z$ with its principal ideal $(z)$ . The norm $N(z)$ equals the ideal norm of $(z)$ .

For 2-and-2 forms, we saw in Proposition 5 that $L$ and $M$ are ideals for a common order $\mathcal{O}$ . For 3-and-1 forms, however, any sublattice $M$ of $\mathbb{Z}[\omega]$ , not necessarily an ideal, with minimal norm $N$ in an appropriate range will yield a tempered perfect form with $\tau^{2}=N$ . Classifying 3-and-1 forms is thus a matter of characterizing the minimal norms that arise for sublattices $M\subset\mathbb{Z}[\omega]$ of prime index $\ell$ .

### 7.1 The Eisenstein integers

In $\mathbb{Z}[\omega]$ , the three pairs of minimal vectors are $\pm 1,\pm\omega,\pm\omega^{2}$ . These six are also the units of $\mathbb{Z}[\omega]$ . The norm $N(a+b\omega)=a^{2}-ab+b^{2}$ .

Let $\mathfrak{p}_{p}$ be a prime ideal of $\mathbb{Z}[\omega]$ over a rational prime $p$ . Write $\mathfrak{p}_{p}=(\pi_{p})$ with $\pi_{p}\in\mathbb{Z}[\omega]$ . One checks that $\mathfrak{p}_{3}=(1-\omega)$ is ramified, meaning $(3)=\mathfrak{p}_{3}^{2}$ . The primes $p\equiv 1\bmod 6$ split: $(p)=\mathfrak{p}_{p}\overline{\mathfrak{p}_{p}}=(\pi_{p})(\overline{\pi_{p}})$ , where $\mathfrak{p}_{p}\neq\overline{\mathfrak{p}_{p}}$ and $N(\pi_{p})=p$ . The primes $p\equiv 5\bmod 6$ remain inert, meaning $\mathfrak{p}_{p}=(p)$ .

We call $x=a+b\omega\in\mathbb{Z}[\omega]$ a primitive representation of $n$ if $gcd(a,b)=1$ and $N(x)=n$ .

#### Proposition 7.

Suppose $n$ is primitively represented by $\mathbb{Z}[\omega]$ . Let $S$ be the set of rational primes $p\equiv 1\bmod 6$ such that $p|n$ . Then the prime factorization of $n$ has the form $3^{r}\prod_{p\in S}p^{r_{p}}$ with $r=0$ or $1$ , and there are $6\cdot 2^{|S|}$ primitive representations of $n$ .

#### Proof.

[15, p. 176]. ∎

### 7.2 Well-rounded sublattices of the Eisenstein integers

#### Proposition 8.

All well-rounded sublattices $M$ of $\mathbb{Z}[\omega]$ with prime index $\ell$ are ideals of $\mathbb{Z}[\omega]$ .

#### Proof.

This is the $L=\mathbb{Z}[\omega]$ case of Proposition 5. ∎

#### Corollary 6.

There are no $3$ -and- $2$ forms and no $2$ -and- $3$ forms.

#### Proof.

If $(L,M)$ is a 3-and- $s^{\prime}$ form for $s^{\prime}\geqslant 2$ , then, by Proposition 8, $M$ is an ideal of $\mathbb{Z}[\omega]$ . Ideals are closed under multiplication by the six units, so $s^{\prime}=3$ . For 2-and-3 forms, apply Proposition 4. ∎

#### Corollary 7.

All $3$ -and- $3$ forms are equivalent to $(L,M)=(\mathbb{Z}[\omega],\mathfrak{p}_{\ell})$ where $\ell=3$ or $\ell\equiv 1\bmod 6$ .

#### Proof.

Since $\mathbb{Z}[\omega]$ is a principal ideal domain, it has exactly one ideal class. This class is well rounded. The rest follows from Corollary 5. ∎

### 7.3 General sublattices of the Eisenstein integers

#### Lemma 5.

Suppose an index $\ell$ sublattice $M$ of $\mathbb{Z}[\omega]$ has linearly independent vectors $v_{1}$ , $v_{2}$ representing positive integers $n_{1}$ , $n_{2}$ both less than or equal to $\ell$ . Then $\{v_{1},v_{2}\}$ is a reduced basis of $M$ .

#### Proof.

Let $\arg(v,w)$ denote the angle between $v$ and $w$ , measured counterclockwise from $v$ . The area of the fundamental parallelogram for $\mathbb{Z}[\omega]$ is $\sqrt{3}/2$ . The pair $\{v_{1},v_{2}\}$ must generate a sublattice $M^{\prime}$ of index at least $\ell$ , hence of area at least $(\sqrt{3}/2)\ell$ . Thus $\|v_{1}\|\|v_{2}\||\sin\arg(v_{1},v_{2})|\geqslant(\sqrt{3}/2)\ell$ with $\|v_{i}\|\leqslant\sqrt{\ell}$ , whence $\arg(\pm v_{1},\pm v_{2})\geqslant\pi/3$ . We may negate $v_{1}$ or $v_{2}$ if necessary to suppose $\pi/3\leqslant\arg(v_{1},v_{2})\leqslant\pi/2$ . Suppose $\{v_{1},v_{2}\}$ as above do not form a reduced basis, so that there exists $v_{3}$ with $\|v_{3}\|<\max(n_{1},n_{2})$ . Then if we consider the order of $v_{1},v_{2},v_{3}$ sweeping counterclockwise from $v_{1}$ , we have two cases:

$$ \displaystyle\arg(v_{1},v_{2})=\arg(v_{1},v_{3})+\arg(v_{3},v_{2})\leqslant\pi/2 \displaystyle\arg(v_{2},-v_{1})=\arg(v_{2},v_{3})+\arg(v_{3},-v_{1})\leqslant 2\pi/3 $$

In the first case either $\arg(v_{1},v_{3})\leqslant\pi/4$ or $\arg(v_{3},v_{2})\leqslant\pi/4$ , a contradiction, since this would imply they generate a sublattice of index smaller than $\ell$ . In the second case, either $\arg(v_{2},v_{3})\leqslant\pi/3$ or $\arg(v_{3},-v_{1})\leqslant\pi/3$ , which is only possible if the sublattice is the principal ideal $(v_{1})$ ; in this case $\{v_{1},v_{2}\}$ would still be a reduced basis, a contradiction. ∎

#### Corollary 8.

Let $v$ be a primitive vector in $\mathbb{Z}[\omega]$ , and suppose $\|v\|^{2}<\ell$ . Then $v$ is contained in exactly one index $\ell$ sublattice $M$ , and $v$ is one of the vectors in a reduced basis of $M$ .

#### Proof.

Lemma 1 gives the existence and uniqueness of $M$ . Since $v$ is primitive, we can complete it to some lattice basis $\{v,w\}$ of $M$ , where $w$ is chosen to be as short as possible. If $\|w\|\geqslant\ell$ , then $\|v\|<\|w\|$ and the basis is reduced. If $\|w\|<\ell$ , the result follows from Lemma 5. ∎

#### Definition 4.

$E_{\ell}(n)$ is the set of all index $\ell$ sublattices of $\mathbb{Z}[\omega]$ that contain a primitive representation of $n$ .

#### Corollary 9.

Let $n<\ell$ be primitively representable. Let $S$ be the set of rational primes $p\equiv 1\bmod 6$ such that $p|n$ . Then $|E_{\ell}(n)|=3\cdot 2^{|S|}$ .

#### Proof.

Let $x_{1}$ and $x_{2}$ be primitive representations of $n$ that are distinct up to units. By Lemma 5, they form a reduced basis of the sublattice they generate. This basis is well rounded. By Proposition 8, however, being distinct up to units, they cannot lie in a common index $\ell$ sublattice. We conclude there is an injective map from primitive representations $x$ of $n$ (up to units) to sublattices $M$ of index $\ell$ . The number of primitive representations $x$ comes from Proposition 7. Since $n$ is either the first or second shortest norm in a given $M$ , we see that for any choice of representation, rotation by roots of unity (except for $\pm 1$ ) generates new sublattices. Thus in total there are $3\cdot 2^{|S|}$ distinct sublattices representing $n$ . ∎

The next results will help determine which $n$ arise as minimal norms represented by index $\ell$ sublattices of $\mathbb{Z}[\omega]$ .

#### Lemma 6.

Suppose $\{v,w\}$ is a reduced basis of an index $\ell$ sublattice $M$ of $\mathbb{Z}[\omega]$ and at least one of the principal ideals $(v)$ , $(w)$ in $\mathbb{Z}[\omega]$ is not divisible by a prime $\mathfrak{p}_{\ell}$ over $\ell$ . Then $(v)$ and $(w)$ share no prime ideals in their factorization.

#### Proof.

Suppose $(v)=\mathfrak{p}(v^{\prime})$ and $(w)=\mathfrak{p}(w^{\prime})$ where $\mathfrak{p}=(u)$ is a prime ideal of $\mathbb{Z}[\omega]$ over $p$ and $v^{\prime},w^{\prime}\in\mathbb{Z}[\omega]$ . Since $v$ and $w$ are primitive, $\mathfrak{p}$ is not inert. Then $\{\bar{u}v,\bar{u}w\}$ generates a sublattice of $\mathbb{Z}[\omega]$ of index $p\ell$ . Hence $\{v^{\prime},w^{\prime}\}$ generates a sublattice of $\mathbb{Z}[\omega]$ of index $\ell/p$ . This implies $p|\ell$ , contradicting the hypothesis. ∎

#### Proposition 9.

Suppose $n_{1}$ , $n_{2}$ are distinct and both $n_{1},n_{2}<\ell$ . Then $|E_{\ell}(n_{1})\cap E_{\ell}(n_{2})|=0$ or $6$ .

#### Proof.

Suppose $M_{1}$ and $M_{2}$ are both in $E_{\ell}(n_{1})\cap E_{\ell}(n_{2})$ . By Lemma 5, they have bases $\{v_{1},w_{1}\}$ and $\{v_{2},w_{2}\}$ where $\|v_{1}\|=\|v_{2}\|=n_{1}$ and $\|w_{1}\|=\|w_{2}\|=n_{2}$ . The principal ideals $(v_{1})$ and $(v_{2})$ differ in their prime ideal factorization only by taking conjugates of certain ideals. If we define $S_{v}$ as the set of prime ideals at which $(v_{1}),(v_{2})$ differ, and $S_{w}$ analogously for $(w_{1}),(w_{2})$ , we may write (relabeling some $\mathfrak{p}_{i}$ as $\overline{\mathfrak{p}_{i}}$ and vice versa if necessary)

$$ (n_{1}n_{2}^{-1})=(v_{1})(v_{2})^{-1}=\prod_{s\in S_{v}}(\overline{\mathfrak{p}_{s}}\mathfrak{p}_{s}^{-1})^{r_{s}}=\prod_{s\in S_{w}}(\overline{\mathfrak{p}_{s}}\mathfrak{p}_{s}^{-1})^{r_{s}}=(w_{1})(w_{2})^{-1}. $$

By Lemma 6, both $\{\mathfrak{p}_{s}\mid s\in S_{v}\}$ and $\{\overline{\mathfrak{p}_{s}}\mid s\in S_{v}\}$ must be disjoint from $\{\mathfrak{p}_{s}\mid s\in S_{w}\}\cup\{\overline{\mathfrak{p}_{s}}\mid s\in S_{w}\}$ . Thus if the two products above are equal, it must be the case that $S_{v}$ and $S_{w}$ are empty. Thus in fact $M_{2}$ differs from $M_{1}$ only by a unit.

Starting with any sublattice, three sublattices are obtained via multiplication by units, and three more obtained via complex conjugation followed by multiplication by units. Thus $|E_{\ell}(n_{1})\cap E_{\ell}(n_{2})|=6$ when it is not $0$ . ∎

### 7.4 Algorithm for 3-and-1 temperaments

Fix a prime $\ell$ , and suppose that one would like to compute all temperaments $\tau$ that correspond to $3$ -and- $1$ forms. $\tau^{2}\in[1,\ell^{2}]$ by Section 3.2. However, we only need to consider half that range:

#### Proposition 10.

All $3$ -and- $1$ forms have $\tau^{2}<\ell$ .

#### Proof.

A 3-and-1 form with temperament $\tau$ can only exist when $L=\mathbb{Z}[\omega]$ has an index $\ell$ sublattice $M$ with reduced basis $\{v,w\}$ with $\|v\|<\|w\|$ and $\|v\|^{2}=\tau^{2}$ . Since we may assume the angle $\theta$ between $v$ and $w$ satisfies $\pi/3\leqslant\theta\leqslant 2\pi/3$ , and because $\|v\|<\|w\|$ , the area of the fundamental parallelogram for $M$ is strictly greater than the area of the fundamental parallelogram for the principal ideal $(v)$ . Therefore $\ell=[\mathbb{Z}[\omega]:M]>[\mathbb{Z}[\omega]:(v)]=\|v\|^{2}$ . ∎

#### Corollary 10.

All $1$ -and- $3$ forms have $\tau^{2}>\ell$ .

#### Proof.

Apply Proposition 4. ∎

The case of $1\leqslant\tau^{2}<(\sqrt{3}/2)\ell$ also has a simple answer, but we require a supporting lemma.

#### Lemma 7.

Let $M$ be an index $\ell$ sublattice of the Eisenstein lattice. Let $v$ be a vector of minimal length within $M$ , and let $w$ be a vector of minimal length in $L-\mathrm{span}(v)$ .

(a) If $\|v\|^{2}\leqslant(\sqrt{3}/2)\ell$ , then $\|w\|^{2}\geqslant(\sqrt{3}/2)\ell$ .

(b) If $\|v\|^{2}\leqslant(3/4)\ell$ , then $\|w\|^{2}\geqslant\ell$ .

#### Proof.

We derived the formula for the area of the parallelogram spanned by $v$ and $w$ during the proof of Lemma 5: $\|v\|\|w\||\sin\theta|=\ell\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ . Suppose $\|v\|^{2}=\mu\ell$ . Then $\|w\|^{2}=\frac{3\ell^{2}}{4\|v\|^{2}\sin^{2}\theta}\geqslant\frac{3\ell^{2}}{4(\mu\ell)(1)}=\frac{(3/4)\ell}{\mu}$ . Both parts follow. ∎

#### Theorem 1.

Let $\ell$ be a prime. For each $\beta\in\mathbb{Z}$ with $\beta<(\sqrt{3}/2)\ell$ which is primitively represented by an element of $\mathbb{Z}[\omega]$ , there is a 3-and-1 form with $\tau^{2}=\beta$ .

#### Proof.

Take $v\in\mathbb{Z}[\omega]$ with $N(v)=\beta$ . By Lemma 1, there is a unique index $\ell$ sublattice $M$ containing $v$ . By Lemma 7 (a), $v$ is (strictly) a minimal vector of $M$ . By Proposition 2, this gives a 3-and-1 form. ∎

We have now characterized the temperaments coming from 3-and-1 forms except in the range $\tau^{2}\in[(\sqrt{3}/2)\ell,\ell]$ . Algorithm 1 below will give us all the $\tau^{2}$ in this range.

Before discussing the algorithm, we need a supporting proposition. Let $M$ be an index $\ell$ sublattice with minimal vector $v=a+b\omega$ . Take $c,d$ such that $ad-bc=1$ . Then $\begin{bmatrix}a&b\\ \ell c&\ell d\end{bmatrix}$ has determinant $\ell$ , which implies by Lemma 1 that the vectors $\{a+b\omega,\ell(c+d\omega)\}$ generate $M$ . Let $w=c+d\omega$ . Without loss of generality, take the angle $\theta$ between $v$ and $w$ to be less than $\pi$ . Let $z\in\mathbb{C}$ be perpendicular to $v$ and of length $\|z\|=\frac{\sqrt{3}\ell}{2\|v\|}$ . Thus $z$ is the height of the parallelogram spanned by $v$ and $\ell w$ . Standard arguments with lattices give the following.

#### Proposition 11.

With $M,v,w,z$ as above, the second shortest vector of $M$ is $\hat{w}=\ell w+tv$ , where $t$ is the nearest integer to $t_{0}=\frac{h-w\ell}{v}\in\mathbb{R}$ .

As we have said, we are now studying the range $\tau^{2}\in[(\sqrt{3}/2)\ell,\ell]$ . However, Algorithm 1 works more naturally on the superset $[(3/4)\ell,\ell]$ . We need the larger range because the inductive mechanism in the algorithm must begin at $(3/4)\ell$ , due to the limitations expressed in Lemma 7.

#### Algorithm 1.

Given a prime $\ell$ , this algorithm determines all temperaments $\tau$ in the range $\tau^{2}\in[(3/4)\ell,\ell]$ that come from 3-and-1 forms. Let $\{\beta_{\alpha}\}_{\alpha=1}^{\infty}$ be the ordered list of integers which are primitively represented as norms of Eisenstein integers, starting with $\beta_{1}=1$ , $\beta_{2}=3$ , $\beta_{3}=7$ , …. Let $n$ be the last index for which $\beta_{n}<(3/4)\ell$ and $N$ the last index for which $\beta_{N}<\ell$ .

- 1. $[$ Create Table $]$ Initialize a list $\mathcal{L}=\{\beta_{n+1},\beta_{n+2},...,\beta_{N}\}$ . In a table format, head the columns with the norms in $\mathcal{L}$ , and, under each norm, write down all primitive vectors representing that norm, where vectors on the list are considered equivalent if they are related by a unit. In effect, each element of the table is a “ $\mathbb{Z}/6\mathbb{Z}$ orbit” of the action of the units. Initialize $T$ , the set of $\tau^{2}$ which will be output, to the empty set.

- 2. $[$ Compute $]$ If $\mathcal{L}$ is empty, output $T$ and terminate the algorithm. Otherwise, choose $v$ under the smallest norm $\beta_{\alpha_{0}}$ available in $\mathcal{L}$ . Using Proposition 11, compute $w$ and its norm $\beta_{\alpha_{1}}$ .

- 3. $[$ Record $]$ Add $\beta_{\alpha_{0}}$ to $T$ .

- 4. $[$ Cross Out $]$ Cross out the $\mathbb{Z}/6\mathbb{Z}$ orbits corresponding to $v$ and $w$ under the norms $\beta_{\alpha_{0}}$ and $\beta_{\alpha_{1}}$ , respectively. If $\beta_{\alpha_{1}}$ is out of range (not on the list), only cross out the orbit corresponding to $v$ . If, after crossing out the orbits, a column has been completely exhausted, delete its corresponding norm from $\mathcal{L}$ . Go to step 2.

#### Proof.

The main hurdle is to check that every vector $v$ chosen in step 2 is in fact the minimal vector of the unique index $\ell$ sublattice that contains $v$ . Once this is verified, the fact that $\beta_{\alpha_{0}}$ is a temperament follows immediately from the definition. To show that the algorithm successfully identifies all of the temperaments in the range, we also need to show that all sublattices with minimal vectors in this range have been identified by the algorithm.

Let $v$ be the first vector chosen by step 2 of the algorithm, and let $M$ be the unique index $\ell$ sublattice that contains $v$ . Due to Corollary 8, $v$ is contained in the reduced basis of $M$ . Let $\hat{w}$ be the other vector in this basis. Suppose that $\|\hat{w}\|<\|v\|$ . Since $v$ has norm $\beta_{n+1}$ , the norm of $\hat{w}$ must be less than $(3/4)\ell$ , which would imply by Lemma 7 (b) that $v$ has norm greater than $\ell$ . Now suppose inductively that after $n$ cycles of steps $1$ through $4$ of the algorithm, all vectors $v$ chosen in step 2 have been minimal vectors. Then we wish to prove that in the $(n+1)$ st cycle, step 2 produces another minimal vector. Suppose that this is not true. Let the true minimal vector be denoted by $\hat{v}$ . Then $\hat{v}$ satisfies $\|\hat{v}\|<\|v\|$ by Proposition 8. It also satisfies $\|\hat{v}\|^{2}>(3/4)\ell$ : otherwise $v$ would have norm greater than $\ell$ by Lemma 7 (b). These bounds imply that $\hat{v}$ was previously dealt with in the algorithm, which means that the orbit corresponding to $v$ should have already been crossed off.

All temperaments are reached by this process by virtue of the correspondence between minimal vectors of index $\ell$ sublattices and $3$ -and- $1$ forms: all minimal vectors of sublattices with norm in the range $[(3/4)\ell,\ell]$ have been identified because of Corollary 8. ∎

## 8 Two-and-two Forms

### 8.1 The Gaussian integers

Before discussing 2-and-2 forms in general, we describe the most common ones, those coming from the Gaussian integers $\mathbb{Z}[i]$ . Since $L=\mathbb{Z}[i]$ is the square lattice, it is well rounded, with $s=2$ . The ring is a principal ideal domain, so it has only one ideal class, the well-rounded class. By Corollary 5, all 2-and-2 forms for $\mathbb{Z}[i]$ have $M$ equal to a prime ideal $\mathfrak{p}_{\ell}$ , where $\ell$ splits or is ramified in $\mathbb{Z}[i]$ , and where $\tau=\sqrt{\ell}$ . The only ramified prime is $\mathfrak{p}_{2}=(1+i)$ . An odd $\ell$ splits if and only if $\ell\equiv 1\bmod 4$ . Since $M$ is an ideal, it is closed under multiplication by $i$ , making it a square lattice in its own right.

#### Remark.

The only well-rounded principal ideals come from the Eisenstein and Gaussian integers. All other 2-and-2 forms will come from orders $\mathcal{O}$ of class number greater than one.

In Figure 4, the dots are $L=\mathbb{Z}[i]$ . The sublattice $M$ of $\odot$ dots is the principal prime ideal $\mathfrak{p}_{17}=(1+4i)$ . The rational prime 17 splits as $\mathfrak{p}_{17}\overline{\mathfrak{p}_{17}}=(1+4i)(1-4i)$ . We have $\ell=17$ and $\tau=\sqrt{17}$ .

### 8.2 Finding all 2-and-2 forms

Two main questions frame our work on 2-and-2 forms. First, given $\ell$ , we wish to show there will be only finitely many 2-and-2 forms up to $\Gamma_{0}(\ell)$ -equivalence. The compactness arguments of [14] already show there are only finitely many, but we prefer a number-theoretic characterization. Corollary 7 answered the corresponding question for 3-and-3 forms. Theorem 1 and Algorithm 1 answered it for 3-and-1 forms.

The second main question is, given an order $\mathcal{O}$ of discriminant $D$ , for which $\ell$ will a 2-and-2 form arise from $\mathcal{O}$ ? This will be answered in Theorem 3.

We now answer the first main question for 2-and-2 forms.

#### Theorem 2.

Fix a prime $\ell$ . Let $D$ be the discriminant of an order $\mathcal{O}$ in an imaginary quadratic number field such that a $2$ -and- $2$ form $(L,M)$ of index $\ell$ arises from a pair of ideal classes in $\mathcal{O}$ . Then

$$ |D|\leqslant 4\ell^{2}. $$

#### Proof.

Let $d<0$ be a squarefree integer. Let $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{d})$ with fundamental discriminant $d_{0}$ . Assume we have a 2-and-2 form whose coefficient ring is an order $\mathcal{O}=\mathcal{O}_{f}\subseteq\mathcal{O}_{K}$ . By Proposition 6, some proper ideal $\mathfrak{p}_{\ell}$ of $\mathcal{O}$ has norm $\ell$ .

By Corollary 2, a class of modules in $\mathcal{O}_{f}$ that is well rounded is ambiguous, that is, has order 1 or 2. By Corollary 5 applied to our 2-and-2 form, $\mathfrak{p}_{\ell}$ carries a well-rounded class to another. Thus $\mathfrak{p}_{\ell}$ itself has order 1 or 2 in the class group. That is, either $\mathfrak{p}_{\ell}$ or $\mathfrak{p}_{\ell}^{2}$ is principal. Take $\alpha\in\mathcal{O}$ so that $(\alpha)=\mathfrak{p}_{\ell}$ or $(\alpha)=\mathfrak{p}_{\ell}^{2}$ in the respective cases. The norm $N(\alpha)$ is $\ell$ or $\ell^{2}$ , respectively.

The argument breaks further into cases. First, suppose $N(\alpha)=\ell$ and $d_{0}\equiv 2,3\bmod 4$ . We may write $\alpha=x+yf\sqrt{d_{0}}$ for $x,y\in\mathbb{Z}$ . Taking norms, $\ell=x^{2}+f^{2}|d_{0}|y^{2}$ . We cannot have $y=0$ because $\ell$ is not a square. Thus $|y|\geqslant 1$ , and we have $f^{2}|d_{0}|=|D|\leqslant\ell$ .

Next, suppose $N(\alpha)=\ell$ and $d\equiv 1\bmod 4$ . We may write $\alpha=x+yf\beta$ where $\beta=\frac{1+\sqrt{d_{0}}}{2}$ . Taking norms, $\ell=(x+yf/2)^{2}+y^{2}f^{2}|d_{0}|/4$ . Again, $y=0$ is impossible, and from $|y|\geqslant 1$ we deduce $|D|\leqslant 4\ell$ .

Next, suppose $N(\alpha)=\ell^{2}$ . If $y\neq 0$ , the same arguments go through, showing that $|D|\leqslant\ell^{2}$ or $|D|\leqslant 4\ell^{2}$ . One extra case is now possible, though: $y=0$ . This is the case where $\mathfrak{p}_{\ell}$ is ramified, that is, $\mathfrak{p}_{\ell}$ is not principal but $\mathfrak{p}_{\ell}^{2}=(\ell)$ . In the ramified case, we must have $\ell\mid D$ . In the rest of the proof, we will show that this last case cannot in fact occur. We state this as

#### Lemma 8.

With the hypotheses of the Theorem, if $\ell$ is odd, then $\ell\nmid D$ .

#### Proof.

Since $\mathfrak{p}_{\ell}\not\sim(1)$ , $L$ and $M$ are in different proper ideal classes.

[5, Prop. 7.3] shows that when $\ell\mid D$ , then among the $\ell+1$ index $\ell$ sublattices of $L$ , there is precisely one that has the same coefficient ring. This must be $M$ . By the same argument, there is precisely one index $\ell$ sublattice of $M$ with the same discriminant, and this must be $\ell L$ .

In fact, however, there are two index $\ell$ sublattices between $L$ and $\ell L$ . This is because $L$ and $M$ have different ideal classes, hence different angles between their minimal vectors. $\tau\neq\sqrt{\ell}$ in this situation. Of the two 2-and-2 forms $(L,M)$ and $(M,\ell L)$ , one of them has $\tau<\sqrt{\ell}$ and the other $\tau>\sqrt{\ell}$ . The contradiction shows $\ell\mid D$ is impossible. ∎

When $\ell=2$ , the analogue of Lemma 8 still holds and is proved by a direct computation. This concludes the proof of Theorem 2. ∎

#### Remark.

The bound $|D|\leqslant 4\ell^{2}$ is apparently not sharp. When we list all the tempered perfect forms for $\ell<100$ , the largest ratio $\frac{|D|}{\ell^{2}}$ occurs at $\ell=47$ , with $D=-6435$ , so that $|D|\approx 2.91\ell^{2}$ . We conjecture that $|D|\leqslant 3\ell^{2}$ in general.

### 8.3 An algorithm for 2-and-2 forms

As a complement to Algorithm 1, we may combine Corollary 5 and Theorem 2 to give an algorithm for finding all 2-and-2 forms whose index is a given prime $\ell$ . Let $D$ run through all the negative discriminants (integers $\equiv 0,1\bmod 4$ ) from $-3$ through $-4\ell^{2}$ . As in Lemma 8, omit $D$ with $\ell\mid D$ . The prime $\ell$ must split, so take only those $D$ with $\left(\frac{D}{\ell}\right)=+1$ . Find all reduced forms of discriminant $D$ ; these are in one-to-one correspondence with the proper ideal classes of the order $\mathcal{O}$ of discriminant $D$ . Identify the well-rounded classes $(a,b,a)$ ; if there are none, skip this $D$ . Identify the class $\mathcal{P}$ that contains $\mathfrak{p}_{\ell}$ ; it is given by the unique reduced form that properly represents $\ell$ . (The prime $\overline{\mathfrak{p}_{\ell}}$ is also in $\mathcal{P}$ , since $\mathcal{P}$ must be an ambiguous class as in the proof of Theorem 2.) Whenever two well-rounded classes $\mathcal{C},\mathcal{C}^{\prime}$ satisfy $\mathcal{C}\mathcal{P}=\mathcal{C}^{\prime}$ , we get a 2-and-2 form, and all 2-and-2 forms of index $\ell$ arise in this way.

## 9 Two-and-two forms from a given order

### 9.1 Which indices appear for a given discriminant

#### Theorem 3.

Let $\mathcal{O}$ be the imaginary quadratic order of discriminant $D=f^{2}d_{0}$ and conductor $f$ . In the proper ideal class group of $\mathcal{O}$ , suppose $\mathcal{C}$ and $\mathcal{C}^{\prime}$ are well-rounded ideal classes. Then for all rational primes $\ell$ for which

$$ \mathrm{a\ proper\ prime\ ideal\ }\mathfrak{p}_{\ell}\mathrm{\ of\ }\mathcal{O}\mathrm{\ is\ in\ the\ class\ }\mathcal{C}^{-1}\mathcal{C}^{\prime}, $$

there exists a $2$ -and- $2$ form for $\ell$ in which the lattices $M\subset L$ are respectively in the classes $\mathcal{C}^{\prime}$ and $\mathcal{C}$ . Infinitely many primes $\ell$ satisfy condition (6).

In the special case where $\mathcal{O}$ has only one ideal class per genus, there is a non-empty set of congruence classes modulo $D$ such that (6) holds if and only if $\ell$ is in one of those congruence classes (apart from a finite number of $\ell$ that are exceptions).

#### Proof.

By Corollary 5, if a prime $\mathfrak{p}_{\ell}$ is in $\mathcal{C}^{-1}\mathcal{C}^{\prime}$ , then there exists a 2-and-2 form for $\ell$ . By the Chebotaryov density theorem, the class $\mathcal{C}^{-1}\mathcal{C}^{\prime}$ contains infinitely many prime ideals.

When there is one class per genus, the statement about congruence classes follows from genus theory as developed by Lagrange and Gauss [8, Thm. 2.26]. The finite number of exceptional $\ell$ are those that divide $D$ . We use only ideals of $\mathcal{O}$ that are relatively prime to $f$ . See [6, (14.43)] when $f=1$ , and see [6, Exer. 18.16] or [8, 7.C] when $f>1$ . ∎

#### 9.1.1 An example with one class per genus

We continue the example of Section 8.3.1. The genus field [6, (15.30)] over $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-1155})$ is $L=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-3},\sqrt{5},\sqrt{-7},\sqrt{-11})$ . The extension $L/\mathbb{Q}$ is Galois with group $(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^{4}$ , and $\mathbb{Q}\subset K\subset L$ . By class field theory, the class number of $K$ will be a multiple of 8, the degree of $L/K$ . Because the class number is exactly 8, the genus field equals the Hilbert class field. This implies [6, (15.33)] that $p$ splits into a principal ideal of $\mathcal{O}_{K}$ if and only if

$$ \left(\frac{-3}{p}\right)=\left(\frac{5}{p}\right)=\left(\frac{-7}{p}\right)=\left(\frac{-11}{p}\right)=1. $$

These four Legendre symbols together give the congruences mentioned in Theorem 3.

For any discriminant $D<0$ , the principal genus consists of the squares in the class group. Since the class group for $D=-1155$ has exponent two, each genus contains exactly one class. By Lagrange’s genus theory [8, 2.C], the $\frac{1}{2}\varphi(1155)=240$ values in $(\mathbb{Z}/1155\mathbb{Z})^{\times}$ with $\left(\frac{D}{\dots}\right)=+1$ are partitioned into eight cosets of 30 values each, each coset being the set of values in $(\mathbb{Z}/1155\mathbb{Z})^{\times}$ which the form can attain.

Our main result for $D=-1155$ is that Hecke operators for $\ell$ will have a 2-and-2 form with this $D$ if and only if $\ell$ is in the values mod 1155 output by one of the two genera $(1,-1,289)$ and $(15,-15,23)$ , which correspond to the classes $(1)$ and $\mathfrak{p}_{23}$ . These values are respectively

$$ \displaystyle 1,4,16,64,169,214,256,289,331,361,379,394,421,466,499,526,529,631, \displaystyle 676,694,709,751,841,856,949,961,991,1024,1054,1114; \displaystyle 23,53,92,113,137,158,212,218,302,317,323,368,422,443,452,533,548, \displaystyle 617,632,653,683,848,863,872,947,977,1037,1082,1103,1142. $$

The first few $\ell$ in these two genera are 23, 53, 113, 137, 317 (in the non-principal genus), 331, 379, 421 (principal genus), 443 (non-principal genus), etc.

#### 9.1.2 An example with two classes per genus

Consider the discriminant $D=-55$ . The class group is $\mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z}$ . The reduced forms are $(1,-1,14)$ , $(2,-1,7)$ , $(2,1,7)$ , and $(4,-3,4)$ . The squares in the class group are $(1,-1,14)$ and $(4,-3,4)$ , so these two constitute the principal genus. The values mod 55 taken by the forms in the principal and non-principal genera are respectively

$$ \underbrace{1,4,9,14,16,26,31,34,36,49}_{\mathfrak{g}}\quad\mathrm{and}\quad 2,7,8,13,17,18,28,32,43,52. $$

Since there is only one well-rounded reduced form, $(4,-3,4)$ , the $\ell$ we need are those in the principal class, because they carry the well-rounded class to itself.

The difficulty, compared to the last example, is that congruence conditions on $\ell$ are not enough to pick out the principal class. If $\ell\in\mathfrak{g}\bmod{55}$ , then we have no way of knowing from this congruence information alone whether $\mathfrak{p}_{\ell}$ is in the principal class or in the $(4,-3,4)$ class.

To distinguish our $\ell$ , we may use the Hilbert class field. The Hilbert class field of $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-55})$ is a $\mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z}$ extension of $K$ and is a quadratic extension of the genus field $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{5},\sqrt{-11})$ . Calculations show that the Hilbert class field is the splitting field of $x^{4}-x^{3}+2x-1$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ and that the four roots of this polynomial are

$$ \varepsilon_{1}\frac{1}{4}\sqrt{5}+\varepsilon_{2}\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{-\varepsilon_{1}\frac{3}{2}\sqrt{5}-\frac{1}{2}}+\frac{1}{4} $$

where $\varepsilon_{1}=\pm 1$ and $\varepsilon_{2}=\pm 1$ independently. See [8, Exercise 6.20].

To determine in practice whether a given $\ell\in\mathfrak{g}\bmod{55}$ is in the principal class, we need not use the Hilbert class field directly. We can simply check whether $x^{2}-xy+14y^{2}$ or $4x^{2}-3xy+4y^{2}$ represents $\ell$ ; it will be one or the other. For instance,

$$ \displaystyle 31 \displaystyle=4(1)^{2}-3(1)(3)+4(3)^{2}\qquad\mathrm{(nonprincipal\ class)} \displaystyle 59 \displaystyle=(1)^{2}-(1)(-2)+14(-2)^{2}\qquad\mathrm{(principal\ class)} \displaystyle 71 \displaystyle=(3)^{2}-(3)(-2)+14(-2)^{2}\qquad\mathrm{(principal\ class)} \displaystyle 89 \displaystyle=4(1)^{2}-3(1)(5)+4(5)^{2}\qquad\mathrm{(nonprincipal\ class)}. $$

The $\ell$ where we see 2-and-2 forms for $D=-55$ are $\ell=59$ , $71$ , etc.

### 9.2 Doubly well-rounded forms have round discriminants

When an order $\mathcal{O}$ has a well-rounded ideal class, we observe that its discriminant $D$ is a product of small primes. When $\mathcal{O}$ has more than one well-rounded class, $D$ is even more strikingly a product of small primes. The first examples of $D$ with two different well-rounded classes are $-1155=-3\cdot 5\cdot 7\cdot 11$ and $-1120=(4)(-2^{3}\cdot 5\cdot 7)$ .

Let $(a,b,c)$ be a reduced form of discriminant $D<0$ . By Lemma 3, the form is well rounded if and only if $a=c$ , implying $D=b^{2}-4a^{2}$ . Thus we would like to know for which discriminants $D<0$ we can solve

$$ D=b^{2}-4a^{2}\quad\mathrm{with\ }|b|\leqslant a\mathrm{\ and\ }(a,b)=1, $$

where the last two conditions are being reduced and primitive. A solution to (7) guarantees by Theorem 3 that there are 2-and-2 forms coming from discriminant $D$ for infinitely many $\ell$ , those in the identity class. Having two or more solutions guarantees there are 2-and-2 forms $(L,M)$ for infinitely many $\ell$ in which $L$ and $M$ come from different classes.

We first suppose $D$ is odd.

#### Proposition 12.

If $D\equiv 1\pmod{4}$ , there is a solution to (7) if and only if $D$ factors as $-FG=D$ with $F,G$ relatively prime and satisfying

$$ \frac{1}{3}\leqslant\frac{F}{G}\leqslant 3. $$

#### Proof.

We have a solution if and only if $-(2a-b)(2a+b)=D$ with $|b|\leqslant a$ and $\gcd(a,b)=1$ . Write $-FG=D$ with $F=2a-b$ and $G=2a+b$ . Clearly $F,G\geqslant 1$ , $\frac{F+G}{4}=a$ , and $\frac{G-F}{2}=b$ . From $|b|\leqslant a$ we obtain $-\frac{F+G}{4}\leqslant\frac{G-F}{2}\leqslant\frac{F+G}{4}$ . By algebra, this gives $\frac{1}{3}\leqslant\frac{F}{G}\leqslant 3$ .

Secondly, $\gcd(a,b)=\gcd\left(\frac{F+G}{4},\frac{G-F}{2}\right)=\gcd\left(\frac{F+G}{4},G\right)$ by adding twice the first argument to the second. Both $F,G$ are odd because their product is odd. Because $G$ is odd, the gcd is unchanged if we multiply the first argument by a power of 2. Hence the gcd is $\gcd(F+G,G)=\gcd(F,G)$ . ∎

#### Examples.

$D=-3$ has a well-rounded lattice (the hexagonal lattice) because $\frac{3}{1}=3$ . This shows the bound in the proposition is sharp.

$D=-55$ has a well-rounded lattice because $\frac{11}{5}=2.2<3$ .

The first case with two solutions is $D=-1155=-3\cdot 5\cdot 7\cdot 11$ . Here $\frac{35}{33}$ is just a little above 1, and $\frac{55}{21}$ is still below 3.

Here is a similar result for even $D$ .

#### Proposition 13.

If $D\equiv 0\pmod{4}$ , there is a solution to (7) if and only if $D$ factors as $-FG=D$ with $F,G$ satisfying

$$ \frac{1}{3}\leqslant\frac{F}{G}\leqslant 3\quad\mathrm{and}\quad\gcd\left(\tfrac{F+G}{2},2G\right)=1. $$

#### Proof.

Here $b$ must be even. Write $b=2b_{1}$ , so $b_{1}^{2}-a^{2}=D/4$ . We have a solution to (7) if and only if $-(a-b_{1})(a+b_{1})=D/4$ with $|b_{1}|\leqslant a/2$ and $\gcd(a,2b_{1})=1$ . Write $-FG=D/4$ with $F=a-b_{1}\geqslant 1$ and $G=a+b_{1}\geqslant 1$ . Solving, $\frac{F+G}{2}=a$ and $\frac{G-F}{2}=b_{1}$ . From $|b_{1}|\leqslant a/2$ we deduce the same formulas $-\frac{F+G}{4}\leqslant\frac{G-F}{2}\leqslant\frac{F+G}{4}\Rightarrow\frac{1}{3}\leqslant\frac{F}{G}\leqslant 3$ as for odd $D$ . ∎

#### Examples.

$D=-4$ with $\frac{1}{1}<3$ and $\gcd(1,4)=1$ .

$D=-32$ with $\frac{4}{2}<3$ and $\gcd(3,4)=1$ .

The first case with two solutions is $D=-1120=(4)(-280)$ , where $-280=-2^{3}\cdot 5\cdot 7$ . Here $\frac{20}{14}=1.429<3$ with $\gcd(17,28)=1$ , and $\frac{28}{10}=2.8<3$ with $\gcd(19,20)=1$ .
